item.title: C# 15: Union Types, Closed Hierarchies, and the One Value™ That Isn't Any of Them
item.description:
.NET 11 launches this week at .NET Conf, and with it comes C# 15. The headline feature, at least for someone like me, is union types. People have been asking for discriminated unions in C# for years, and now there’s a union keyword in the language.

A disclaimer before we start: C# is not my home turf. I write Elm on the frontend, I’ve done a fair bit of Kotlin, and I hope to write a lot more F#. So this is an outsider looking at a feature I care about, in a language I don’t use daily. If I’ve missed some well-known C# idiom below, I’d genuinely like to hear about it.

item.title: Go 1.27: encoding/json/v2, Stricter Defaults, and Finally [] for Nil Slices
item.description:
The Go team just shipped encoding/json/v2 as stable in Go 1.27. It’s been available behind GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2 since 1.25, and I’ve been meaning to try it ever since (I never got around to it). So now I finally did.

First of all: I have some mixed feelings about encoding/json. It works fine most of the time, but it also accepts quite a lot of stuff it shouldn’t, without telling you. Coming from Elm, where a decoder fails the moment something doesn’t match, v1 always felt a bit too forgiving for my taste. v2 is a lot stricter, and I like it!

item.title: Ktor 3.4.0: HTML Fragments, HTMX, and Finally Proper SSE Cleanup
item.description:
Ktor 3.4.0 just dropped, and while there’s a laundry list of new features, a few of them made me genuinely excited. One of them even feels like a direct response to that SSE post I wrote where we accidentally DDoS’d ourselves. (It’s not, of course. But let me have this.)

HTML Fragments: Ktor Gets HTMX-Friendly Link to heading

If you’ve been following the HTMX movement (and if you haven’t, you’re missing out on some delightfully old-school-yet-modern web development), you know that the whole point is to return HTML fragments from your server, not full pages. Swap out a <div>, update a table row, replace a form with a success message. Simple stuff.

item.title: Kotlin's Rich Errors: Native, Typed Errors Without Exceptions
item.description:
At KotlinConf 2025, the Kotlin team showcased progress toward Rich Errors with union types. After years of watching languages slowly adopt patterns that Elm has championed since day one, it’s exciting to see Kotlin taking this significant step toward more explicit, type-safe error handling. And in a very “native” Kotlin way at that!
